opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest about where the frontier labs are going to win, because they're going to win a lot of places. If your whole business is "we wrap the best model and add a nice prompt," you're building on sand. Every time the next model comes out, a chunk of your value proposition just evaporates. So you have to ask: what does the model getting better *help* me with, rather than what does it replace?

The way I'd frame it is that the labs are building general capability, and general capability is necessary but not sufficient for an agent to actually do useful work in the real world. What's missing is context. An agent that's going to do real work in a specific domain needs to know how that business works, what the data looks like, what the edge cases are, what "good" means to the customer. A lot of that isn't on the internet and isn't in the pretraining data. It lives in workflows, in people's heads, in systems that are messy and proprietary. If you can be the company that captures that context and connects it to the model, you're in a much more defensible position.

The second thing is that reliability is the whole game for agents. A demo that works 80% of the time is impressive. A product that works 80% of the time is useless for most real tasks, because someone has to check everything anyway. Getting from 80 to 99 is mostly not a raw intelligence problem. It's evaluation, it's understanding failure modes in your specific domain, it's building the right scaffolding, the right checkpoints where a human comes in, the right way to recover from errors. That's grinding, unglamorous work, and the frontier labs generally aren't going to do it for every vertical. They can't. There are too many.

Third, I'd pick a domain where the feedback loop is tight and the value of a completed task is really legible. If you can say "this agent closed this ticket" or "this agent reconciled these accounts" and the customer can see the dollars, you can charge for outcomes rather than seats or tokens. That aligns you with the customer and it also means that as the models get cheaper and better, your margins go up instead of your product getting commoditized.

And finally, you want to design so you're riding the wave. Assume the model in a year will be dramatically better. Build the product so that improvement flows straight through to your customers, and don't over-engineer around today's limitations, because those workarounds become technical debt the moment the next model ships. The companies that do well will be the ones where a new frontier model release is great news, not an existential threat.

r001.rationale: The response recommends domain-specific agents built around business context and workflows, but does not say they should involve other people rather than serve an individual's computer-based productivity.

r002.rationale: It describes domain context and reliability as defensible advantages, but does not state that agent businesses rely on the same kinds of moats as conventional businesses.

r003.rationale: The response does not recommend choosing a business that can generate network effects.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing you have to accept is that you're not going to compete with the frontier labs on the model. That's just not the game. The labs are going to keep pushing capabilities, and if your whole business is a thin layer on top of the model, every new release is going to eat a piece of what you built. I saw this from the inside at OpenAI. Every time we shipped a new model, there was a set of startups whose core feature just became a default behavior.

So the question becomes, where does the value actually live if it's not in the model? And I think the answer is that it lives in the boring stuff. It lives in the context. The agent that wins in, say, legal or insurance or logistics is the one that knows how that particular business actually works. What are the weird edge cases? What does the data look like? Which systems does it have to talk to, and what breaks when you try to talk to them? The labs are never going to go deep enough on any one of those domains to really understand it. They can't. They're building a general thing.

The second piece is the workflow. Agents are only useful once they're actually doing the work end to end. Not answering a question, but closing the ticket, filing the claim, updating the system of record. And getting there means you have to do a lot of unglamorous integration work, and you have to earn trust incrementally. Nobody hands an agent the keys to their business on day one. You start with a narrow task, you make it reliable, you show the error rate is low, and then they let you do a little more. That trust is the real asset, and it compounds in a way that's very hard for a new entrant to replicate, even if that new entrant has a better model.

The third thing I'd say is that you want to be a beneficiary of the model progress, not a victim of it. So you design your product so that when the next model comes out, your agent just gets better. You've got the evals, you've got the data, you've got the harness around it. You swap the model in and your customers wake up to a better product. If the frontier labs are spending billions to make your product better for free, that's a great position to be in.

And then, honestly, the last piece is just distribution and sales. The labs are good at a lot of things, but they are not set up to go sit with a mid-sized insurance company for six months and figure out how to deploy this thing. Someone has to do that. And that person ends up owning the customer relationship, which in enterprise software has always been where the money is.

So the short version is: don't compete on intelligence. Compete on understanding the problem, owning the workflow, and being the one the customer actually trusts.

r001.rationale: The response recommends agents that handle end-to-end business workflows, integrate with company systems, and earn trust from enterprise customers, rather than individual productivity tools.

r002.rationale: It identifies integration, compounding customer trust, and sales and customer relationships as durable advantages, comparing the latter to where value has traditionally lived in enterprise software.

r003.rationale: The response does not recommend choosing a business that can generate network effects.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with a customer problem where the model is only one part of the solution. If your entire product is something the next model release can do out of the box, you’re in a pretty fragile position.

Look for a workflow where you can own the whole outcome. That means understanding how the customer works, connecting to their systems, knowing what a good result looks like, and handling the cases where the agent gets stuck. There’s a lot of work between a model that can demonstrate a task and a product somebody trusts to do that task every day. That’s where you can build a business.

You also want better models to help you. If each improvement lets you automate more of the workflow, improves your margins, and makes your customers happier, then the frontier labs are effectively supplying you with a better component.

So I’d pick a fairly narrow market, work closely with a few customers, and build a way to measure whether you’re actually delivering the outcome they care about. Over time, those customer relationships, integrations, and the ability to evaluate performance can become a real advantage. The question is less, ‘How do I beat a frontier lab?’ and more, ‘What can I deliver for this customer that a general-purpose model alone doesn’t?’

r001.rationale: The response recommends owning a customer workflow and outcome, but does not say the agents should involve other people rather than serve an individual's computer-based productivity.

r002.rationale: It names customer relationships, integrations, and evaluation as potential advantages, but does not state that agent businesses rely on the same kinds of moats as conventional businesses.

r003.rationale: The response does not recommend choosing a business that can generate network effects.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start with a customer problem where getting the work done is really valuable, and where you can tell whether the agent actually succeeded. I wouldn’t start with, “We have an agent; what can we sell?” I’d look for a workflow that people already spend a lot of time and money on, and figure out how much of that workflow you can own.

The frontier labs have an advantage in building the underlying models. But building a model and delivering a reliable service inside a particular business are different problems. You need the integrations, the context, the permissions, and a way to handle exceptions. You need to understand what the customer considers a good result. There’s a lot of product work in that gap.

And I’d design the business to benefit as the models improve. If a better model comes out tomorrow, you want that to make your product more useful and your economics better. If it makes your product unnecessary, I’d be worried.

So the question is: what are you accumulating as customers use the product? It might be a better understanding of their workflow, a set of evaluations that captures what actually matters, or distribution into a market that’s hard to reach. You want a reason customers choose you that survives the next model release.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on valuable customer workflows and reliable service, but does not recommend agents involving other people rather than individual computer productivity.

r002.rationale: It names workflow understanding, evaluations, and market distribution as possible advantages, but does not state that durable AI-agent advantages are the same kinds of moats as conventional businesses.

r003.rationale: It recommends accumulating workflow knowledge, evaluations, or distribution, but does not recommend choosing a business that can generate network effects.
